Official repo: github.com/lemomo-ai/lemo-opuscar · by Lemomo ( @lemomo_ai )
Every frame, every note and every cut was written in code by Claude Opus 5.5. ▶ Watch · All 98 styles · Download 1080p
I'm Lemomo ( @lemomo-ai ). More about me on my profile.
Not an awesome list. Every film here was made by me, with Claude Opus 5.5. The styles are tuned for Opus 5.5; other models may not reproduce them.
Every film was directed, drawn, scored and mixed by an AI agent writing code:
🎨 Picture : canvas and WebGL pages, rendered frame by frame
🎵 Music : original scores from free sample libraries
Option 1: install the skill (recommended)
On first use it downloads the guides, tools and style prompts to ~/lemo-opuscar , shared by all your films.
Each film's project, from source to finished video, goes in the folder you started from.
For other agents, copy plugin/skills/lemo-opuscar/ into their skills folder.
Make a 45-second film in the watercolor style about the coffee farm my family runs. Warm female narrator.
Make a 40-second LiDAR Survey film about the old quarry in the hills behind our town, from public laser-scan data.
Name the style in English or Chinese; the style index lists them all.
Not sure yet? With the skill installed, type /lemo-opuscar:lemo-opuscar and nothing else. It asks which language to use, then what you'd like to do: a film in a library style, make a style your own , or a film in a style you've saved.
anything it can't decide about your topic;
whether you have your own voice, music or other material ;
whether you want to see a storyboard first. Say yes and it stops once to show you the key shots in the real style; otherwise it goes straight to the finished film.
The agent reads three guides and works like a small studio:
Everyone wants something different: their own brand colours, logo, characters, the tone of their channel. Now you can change a library style into one that's only yours, or make one from a blank page that the library doesn't have. It's the same process I use to add a new style to the library.
Two ways in. Pick one after starting the skill, or say it in one line:
I want to change the Ukiyo-e style into my own version.
Start from a blank page: a chalk-on-blackboard style, warm and slow.
Change a library style : it lists every style with the gallery link, and you type the one to change.
Start from a blank page : describe the look in your own words, or share a picture or a film you like. Claude picks the closest library style as the technique base, tells you why, and you agree or pick another.
Plan it one question at a time. Each question has a few options, the recommended one first, with the reason. Roughly: what it's for: what kind of films, which platform (vertical feeds want 1080×1920 or 1080×1440), any brand colours, logo, fonts or recurring characters; what to change: for a library style it first sorts the style into three groups, safe to change (palette, type, pace, sound, signature moves), changes its character (materials and rendering, the colour logic, camera grammar) and can't change (the style's essence: change that and it's a different style); which way to take each part, and last, a name. Vague is fine: say "more premium" or "livelier" and it turns that into concrete changes to pick from. Too slow? Choose "free conversation", the last option on every question, and just talk it through; say "you decide" at any point and it fills in the rest with its recommendations. At most five changes a round when changing a library style; everything is drawn in code, no image generation.

See one style frame first , drawn with the real code. When you changed a library style, the same frame is rendered in the original too, side by side: original left, yours right. Say what's off; if it still isn't right after two rounds, it says so and suggests a closer base.

A 15–30 second demo film. Every change is on screen, with music and sound effects. It checks the film and fixes it once before handing it over.

Keep it when you're happy. It asks: keep it as my style, another round, or not now. Until you say yes, everything stays in that project's folder.

Once kept, the style lives in ~/lemo-my-styles/ / , shaped like a library style: the style prompt, what changed, the demo film and its source, so later films can reuse the techniques. Then name it like any other style: "Make a 30-second film in my Night Ukiyo-e style about…" . When you pick a style, your own are listed first.
Library updates and reinstalling never touch them. When the base style is updated later, Claude mentions it once and asks whether to bring the useful fixes into your copy. The steps Claude follows are in MY-STYLES.md .
A film takes an agent about 30–60 minutes and a fair amount of tokens.
You need Node 20+, ffmpeg 7+ and Python 3.11+ (or uv ); the agent installs the rest. Ubuntu 24.04 ships ffmpeg 6.1, which is too old: use a static build .
Default output 1920×1080, 24 fps; other sizes on request.
Update, then restart Claude Code (the library in ~/lemo-opuscar updates itself on the next film):
After an update, ask for a film as usual; to make a style your own, see above .
Your own styles in ~/lemo-my-styles/ stay through updates and uninstalls; delete that folder yourself if you don't want them.
A thank-you film at each milestone, made in code like everything here. Click a poster to watch on the thank-you page .
Demo films and their stills (in styles/ , the gallery and the Releases): CC BY 4.0 . You may share, adapt and use them commercially; credit LemoLab with a link to this repository, and say if you changed them.
Films you make with the library : yours, no credit needed.
Third-party assets in the demos : they keep their own licences (see each demo's CREDITS ).
Three voice tracks are not CC BY 4.0 : the shouts in Game Show Flat (macOS system voices, say ), the narration in Paper-cut Lightbox (Microsoft Edge TTS), which will be re-voiced with Kokoro, and the narration in Broadcast News Package (Doubao TTS, under Volcengine's terms). They are excluded from the licence above. Don't reuse them; in your own films use Kokoro (the default) or a voice you have the right to use.
You are responsible for the materials you use in your films.
